name: Hinokitiol / thujaplicin

lead: Hinokitiol (beta-thujaplicin) is a natural compound from the heartwood of hinoki cypress and western red cedar. It appears in Japanese and other cosmetic products such as hair tonics, shampoos, skin lotions and toothpastes, where it is used for its antimicrobial properties and as a cosmetic preservative.

People using it aim for a cleaner scalp, fresher breath and calmer skin. Research on hinokitiol is mostly laboratory and animal work; a small randomized pilot study of a hinokitiol gel on oral malodor and a 2008 report on hair growth from a nanocapsule preparation are among the human-related findings.

paras: It is used as an ingredient in commercial rinse-off and leave-on products rather than taken as a drug. Cosmetic forms listed include soaps, lotions, shampoos, hair tonics, eyelid cleansers, toothpastes and breath sprays.

It is a food additive in Japan and a cosmetic ingredient, with a rat study in 2006 finding no carcinogenic effect. Strong chelating and ionophore activity is the subject of laboratory work. Little clinical safety data exists for concentrated use.

angle.text: Hinokitiol is included in cosmetic products for hair, skin and oral care because of its antimicrobial activity. A 2008 report described hair growth in an animal model from a nanocapsule preparation.

lead: Hinokitiol, also called beta-thujaplicin, is a monoterpenoid tropolone found in the heartwood of Cupressaceae trees such as Taiwanese hinoki and western red cedar. Chemist Tetsuo Nozoe isolated it in 1936, and Ralph Raphael synthesized it in 1951. [1]

In appearance care it turns up in soaps, skin lotions, shampoos, hair tonics, toothpastes and breath sprays. [1][2] Manufacturers use it for antimicrobial and preservative functions, and products position it for scalp care, fresher breath and skin care.

Its biological activity, including iron and zinc binding, has been studied in cells and animals. [1][3] Human data relevant to looks are small, such as a pilot trial of a hinokitiol gel for oral malodor. [4]

paras: It is listed as an ingredient in soaps, skin lotions, eyelid cleansers, shampoos and hair tonics, and in toothpastes and breath sprays. [1] A 2008 study reported promotion of hair growth in vivo with a cosmetic preparation using hinokitiol-loaded nanocapsules. [1]
It has been used as a wood preservative, insect repellent and food additive, and traditional Japanese buildings using hinoki wood have resisted decay for centuries. [1]

Hinokitiol reversibly binds metals such as iron, zinc and copper and acts as an ionophore and iron chelator. [1] A 2017 Science study reported that it restored iron transport and promoted absorption and hemoglobinization in animals. [3] Reviews describe antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and anticancer effects mainly in cells. [5]
Nozoe isolated it in 1936 from Taiwanese hinoki oil; the same compound was reported from western red cedar in 1948 and named beta-thujaplicin. A synthetic route was achieved in 1951. [1][2]

A 2006 rat study found no carcinogenic effect, and Canada categorized the compound in 2006 as non-persistent and non-bioaccumulative. [1] Clinical evidence supporting the laboratory findings is limited. [1]

A randomized, open-label pilot study of 18 participants compared a hinokitiol-containing gel with a gel without it for mouth cleaning and oral malodor. [4] A clinical trial of beta-thujaplicin ear drops in 31 dogs with Malassezia-related otitis externa has also been published. [6] A 2008 report on hair growth involved a nanocapsule preparation. [1] No trials of hinokitiol for hair loss in people were identified.
